messages.author: 641ba92c5c408935
messages.subject: Second-order model implementation
parts:
Good day,

Thank you for a great package, which I am learning slowly but surely.

I have tried to specify a second-order model with four first-order factors as indicators. But the Rhat's for the second-order loadings are very high and the direction of the loadings are also negative when they should be positive. The first-order std factor loadings also seem lower to me compared to a first-order only model, by about 0.15 to 0.20. 

Perhaps it is just a specification issue of the model on my side. But the second-order model does work as would be expected in other software with frequentist methods. 

Here is the model, the output is in the attached text file if needed. 

model1 <- 'EX =~ batEX1 + batEX2 + batEX3 + batEX4 + batEX5 + batEX6 + batEX7 + batEX8
           MD =~ batMD1 + batMD2 + batMD3 + batMD4 + batMD5
           CC =~ batCC1 + batCC2 + batCC3 + batCC4 + batCC5
           EC =~ batEC1 + batEC2 + batEC3 + batEC4 + batEC5
           
           bat =~ EX + MD + CC + EC'

model1.fit <-  bcfa(model1, data=batdata, std.lv=T, 
                    n.chains = 3, burnin=20000, 
                    sample=2000)

Thank you for your time.

messages.subject: Re: Second-order model implementation
parts:
Leon

Yes, as long as all the factor loadings go in the same direction it does match your hypothesis, but the factor means the opposite direction of what you expected. For example, if your factor were depression, with negative factor loadings means lack of depression.
You can set the direction of the factor by fixing one of the factor loadings to be positive, then the rest should follow

bat =~ L1*EX + MD + CC + EC
L1 > 0

Like adding this cobstraint to the model

parts:
Leon,

I have not had a chance to run this model but had a couple thoughts:

- It is possible that chains sometimes get stuck on the wrong side of zero, and this goes away upon re-running the model. Sometimes adding the argument inits="simple" can help.

- The thing about sign indeterminacy (from Mauricio) suggests that priors like normal(0,big variance) are not appropriate, because you are expecting the loadings to all be positive. So setting different prior distributions might also help. For details on doing that, see

https://ecmerkle.github.io/blavaan/articles/prior.html


Ed

messages.subject: Re: Second-order model implementation
parts:
Ed / Mauricio,

Just reporting back.

The specification of inits = "simple" worked for the signs of the loading on the factors.

I then used inits = "prior" and specified some different priors and also added both std.lv and std.ov to TRUE as I wanted to use standardized priors. This then again had a lot of warnings, but this was my mistake due to the priors as I never set intercept priors and they were the standard (0,35), but setting them to (0,1) worked for the model. 

Then I tried a model with specific standardized priors on the loadings to say, well I know all these loadings are positive. The prior on the loadings of (.5,.5) caused trouble for these factor loadings as I got warnings and bad Rhats, so I also tried (.5,.15) and these presented no problems after the estimation. 

Lastly, I added approximately zero cross-loadings with (0,.05) and (0,.01) and both of these were bad on the cross-loadings. I then changed this to (0,.10) and the model worked. I also tried a model with a higher expectation of the second-order factor loadings (.7, .15) and this also worked. 

Thanks!

When using tighter priors such as N(0.7, 0.15), make sure the posterior distribution is not being constrainted much by the prior
For example check the 95% interval from the prior, and see that the posterior is not too close to it

quantile(rnorm(10000, mean=0.7, sd=0.15), probs=c(.025, .0975))
